Gaurav started by sowing vegetables on a friend's farm in Landran, for he himself did not own any land. Chalking out plans to market his produce in the tri-city of Chandigarh, Mohali and Panchkula, he says he will foray into producing exotic vegetables, fruits and wheat among other crops.

Harpal Singh Grewal, who has brought his 40-hectare farm in Sirsa under organic farming, claims that as per a Massachusetts University study, natural farming has the capacity to produce a yield three times higher than the chemical methods. Sixty-two-year-old Grewal claims he also exports his produce to the USA and Canada. Worried over the unchecked use of chemical sprays, he says, "I wonder why they call it agriculture. It should be termed as chemiculture."

It was the fear of eating poisonous vegetables that were grown on the banks of Buddha Nullah that made Jaskirat Singh, a 31-year-old mechanical engineer-turned-software expert, to go organic.

"When I read about the toxic contents in the vegetables that we were eating, I decided to start organic farming at a small-scale," says Jaskirat, who took on lease three acres of land near Guru Nanak Dev Engineering College. "Selling software is my bread and butter. But growing organic crops is a way of life. I am not doing it for commercial gains. I want to produce it on a large-scale. At present, we have no choice but to buy the products that are being sold in the market."

But it was not an easy ride for Jaskirat. "First, I needed organic seeds for my crop which were provided by Jaitu-based Kheti Virasat Mission. The first year of experiment yielded crop with which I could feed my family. This year the rains destroyed everything but I have replanted the fields," he says. Jaskirat, who is growing maize and a few vegetables, says, "This winter I want organic saag and organic makki ki roti on my dinning table."

Farmers, who do not have grand degrees, are also going the organic way. For Bir Davinder of Dabri Khana village, non-organic wheat is poisonous. "Zeher wali kanak de rate de mukable saadi kanak (organic wheat) da mul dugna hai (As compared to the 'poisonous wheat', our wheat fetches double price)," says Bir Davinder. "I have been doing it for the last three years and the results are remarkable," he says.

Amarjit Sharma of Chaina village is also part of the organic club.

"I have sown organic cotton for the third time and will be sowing wheat for the fourth time," says Sharma, who has turned his five acres organic. "With this, there has been a considerable decrease in the input costs," tells Sharma.

According to Umendra Dutt, executive director of Jaitu-based Kheti Virasat Mission (KVM), an NGO that pioneered organic farming in the region, educated youths have taken a shine to the concept. "From less than 1,000 acres last year, the farmers associated with us have increased the area under cultivation to 2,000 acres this year," claims Dutt, adding that KVM has also been promoting city farming culture, where people are encouraged to grow vegetables and other crops on small-scale in their houses. "We have advocates, doctors, engineers and people from other walks of life doing city farming in Chandigarh and Ludhiana," Dutt says.

Heading: On a mission against chemical farming - Indian Express
Content:
Thirty-two-year-old homoeopath Dr Harminder Singh Sidhu's two acres of ancestral land in Zalaldiwal village, near Raikot, was lying unutilised for the past 25 years. "I started farming one-and-a-half years ago and am happy with the returns. Every morning I spend four hours at my farms and then leave for my Ghumar Mandi clinic in Ludhiana."

"I learnt this skill from a few farmers, says Dr Sidhu, adding that the expenditure involved in natural farming is less and the returns are high.

Dr Harminder Singh, a homoeopath from Jalaldiwal village in Ludhiana district had put the thinking cap on after a number of patients with stomach and intestine problems started thronging his clinic. "I found that the cause of all the diseases was pesticides that had entered the food chain," says Dr Harminder, who, besides using the organic produce grown on about two acres for home use, also markets it in Ludhiana.

"Patients with swelling in abdomen, coeliac diseases and hormonal imbalance come to me in large numbers. Some kids complain of underdeveloped abdomens, while others are underweight," says Dr Harminder, while stressing the need to adopt organic farming to avoid various health complications. "I encourage farmers to switch over to organic farming on at least an acre and see the difference," he adds.

For a successful endoscopic surgeon and owner of Bawa Hospital in Jalandhar, organic farming is a passion.

Coming from a family of farmers, Dr Paramjit Singh Bakshi takes out sufficient time for his obsession. He started cultivating aloe vera, which is also called 'Lily of Desert', on 16 acres in kandi area of Hoshiarpur district with the help of the Forest Department. About three years ago, he had set up a processing plant, 'Global Herbs', in Varyana village, Jalandhar. "At present, we produce aloe vera juice, but will soon start producing gel and powder," he says.

"Being a doctor, I was aware of the ill-effects of chemical farming. I own a vermicompost plant and use only organic manure in my fields," he says, adding that he is also planning to export aloe vera.

For Dr Sandeep Saini of Hoshiarpur district, who was a dental surgeon in PGI and senior lecturer in Adesh Pratap Dental College and Research, Bathinda, organic farming is his favourite pastime.

He started it over a year ago in his native village, Lambra Kangri, and Dr Saini's hobby has been fruitful with a healthy crop of maize, wheat and various vegetables. His father, Madan Lal, who has been attending various camps on organic farming has been a great help.

Most of the farmers in the state want high yield, they are not concerned about the harmful affect of the chemical fertilisers, Dr Saini says. "Punjab is the largest user of fertilisers, the affect of which is seen in form of various diseases. Organic farming, on the other hand, is a zero-budget or debt-free farming. Cow dung is used as a fertiliser, while neem serves the pesticide. It takes about three years for the land to be free from the effects of chemical fertilisers. However, in the first year of the organic farming, the chemical effects are reduced by about 60 per cent," he says.

"I have been advising all my friends to adopt natural way of farming to prevent various diseases," he says.

Heading: PSEB edge past CFHA - Indian Express
Content:
The Punjab Organic Farming Association (POFA) was formed recently by 60 like-minded people, including farmers, professors, doctors and engineers. A large number of farmers from as many as 19 districts of the state have shown eagerness to join the mission. The convener of POFA, Jaspal Singh, says the indifferent attitude of successive state governments towards agriculture sector resulted in its dependence on fertilisers.

"This led to the entry of corporate houses, which are interested only in making money at the cost of environment and society," he says.

He says the Punjab government is yet to spare a thought for bringing a paradigm shift in the agriculture sector. POFA endeavours to mobilise farmers for popularising organic farming.

"We have urged the government to provide infrastructure, training and funds for organic farming. And most importantly, provide marketing support for produce," says Jaspal.

Heading: Rains in HP threaten floods in state - Indian Express
Content:
In a highly thrilling match, Punjab State Electrical Board (PSEB) edged out CFH Academy by 2-1 in the 38th SN Vohra's All India Gurmit Memorial Hockey Tournament being played at Sector 42 Hockey Stadium on Sunday.

Displaying an attacking game, players from both the team tried their best to put their respective team in the advantage. However, it was PSEB who broke the deadlock in the 19th minute when shirt number nine Yadwinder Singh converted a penalty corner into goal to send his team into frenzy. Amrik Singh doubled the lead in the 33rd minute when he also scored through a penalty corner. However, Gurjant Singh led CFHA's recovery when he scored a goal and reduced the deficit to 2-1 in the 49th minute. PSEB played a dominating game throughout the match was evident from the fact that PSEB earned seven penalties in reply to nil by CFHA.

Heading: Gobind Sagar reservoir touches danger mark - Indian Express
Content:
15 villages affected due to overflowing Ghaggar; alert sounded in Patiala

Heavy rains that had spread devastation in Himachal Pradesh are now threatening many parts of Punjab. With rainwater from Himachal flowing into the Ghaggar and its level nearing the danger mark, a flood alert has been sounded in Patiala and Sangrur districts.

At least 15 villages have been badly affected in Rajpura tehsil of Patiala after waters from the 25 dara nullah flowing into the Ghaggar entered the hamlets in the wee hours today.

Though no loss of life has been reported, the standing paddy crop in the villages has been damaged.

As the water level of Ghaggar in Ghanour and Khanouri areas is near the danger mark, a fresh flood alert has been sounded and the villagers have been told to evacuate. Sources said the water level in Ghaggar at Sarala Kalan village in Ghanour had crossed the 17.5 feet mark, 1.5 feet above the danger mark, and though it has now started receding, it was still a cause for worry.

At Khanouri, bordering Haryana, the water level in Ghaggar has risen to 752.8 feet, touching the danger mark of 753 feet. Sources said overflowing water in the Ghaggar created at least three 50 to 90 feet breaches in Rajpura at Mehdoodan, Kaami Kalan and Lacchhru villages. Besides, other affected villages included Raipur, Bhathunia Khurd, Kauni Khurd, Maanheri and Sarala.

If more rains lash the region, authorities fear the situation would worsen.

Heading: Kidney racket: 8 agents held - Indian Express
Content:
Water at Gobind Sagar reservoir touched the flood level at the 1,680 feet mark, while the Pong Dam reservoir is just two feet below the danger mark and the Ranjit Sagar Dam 25 feet lower than the flood level.

However, Chief Engineer, Drainage, Ashok Malhotra says there is nothing to panic. "The discharge in the Sutlej has fallen from 90,000 cusecs yesterday to 65,000 cusecs, so the river is under control. Even at the Gobind Sagar Dam, we still have a margin of about five feet and whatever water we have at the moment can be used for power generation," he says.

However, the officials admit that much depends on the rainfall in Himachal Pradesh and even Punjab, "for if we get more water from HP, we will have no option but release it".

The officials at the Bhakra Beas Management Board seem to be working overtime to use up all the extra water. BBMB Chief Engineer S C Jain says, "The situation is under control. We are running all our machines full-time. Bhakra will work to its full generation capacity of 1,325 mega watts, which means there will be no power cuts in the state." Jain adds, "At present, there is no question of releasing water ."

Heading: This multiple sclerosis patient has altruistic nerve - Indian Express
Content:
The district police claim to have busted a kidney racket with the arrest of eight members of a gang of agents.

The accused-- identified as Sukhdev Kumar, Jatinder Kumar, Suresh Kumar, Paramjit Singh, Sonu, Vijay, Shekhar and Ali Mohammed-- were nabbed from a liquor shop following a raid.

Sources said the police had received information that the accused were roaming near the Amritsar Medical College campus, looking for prey.

Police sources said the accused had sold their kidneys prior to becoming members of the gang. They used to send unemployed youths to Bihar, where they were forced to sell their kidneys.

Heading: BSF shoots down 4 Bangla nationals - Indian Express
Content:
For 30-year-old Guneet Veer Bawa, lovingly called Kaku Bawa, life began after multiple sclerosis, a debilitating disease that hit his nervous system a decade ago.

The ailment, according to doctors, can be fatal at times. But Bawa has mastered the art of living with his disability, and has made it his mission to tutor other sufferers. He plans to open a chain of schools for special children to help them live life to the fullest.

His schools in Amritsar have won Bawa a couple of honours, including Bharat Jyoti Award, which was conferred on him by India International Friendship Society. He has also been conferred the Rashtriya Ratna Award.

"My doctor tells me that the disease is very serious and I should tread carefully. But with my courage and strong will power, I have overcome all hurdles in life," says Bawa.

"I was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis when I was all of 20. The initial days were very shattering, but I realised that this is where life begins, and not ends," he says.

He says initially he used to hide the fact that he is suffering from the disease due to the stigma attached to it, but then he thought that he should come out and help others.

"Multiple sclerosis is not as common in India as it is in the US. Here, we have not more than 12 patients across the country. They usually come to me for counseling," says Bawa, who is running a nationwide forum for such patients. His father, Squadron Leader R S Bawa (retd), says his son has been financially independent since teenage and wants to help children with special abilities lead an independent life.

"His first earning of Rs 20,000 came after he organised a painting exhibition when he was 14-year-old," says the proud father.

Heading: Badal makes case for 10 pc quota for rural poor students - Indian Express
Content:
The Border Security Force, led by Company Commander Chiman Rana, today shot dead four Bangladeshis, who were attempting to cross over to the Pakistani territory.

According to information, at 6 am today, at the time of change of guard duty, four men were spotted crossing the barbed fence between Ameeran and Maujam checkposts.

When the BSF jawans asked them to stop, they ran towards the Pakistani territory, following which they were shot dead, about 20 yards inside the Indian territory.

"Bangladeshi passports were found in their luggage," BSF DIG V K Sharma said. However, the BSF refused to divulge the names on the passports "due to security reasons".

No weapon was recovered from them, sources said. "The Bangla nationals seem to have got training in crossing the fencing, as it is very hard to cross without getting a scratch on the body," the DIG added.

Heading: Truck carrying adulterated salt confiscated in Amritsar - Indian Express
Content:
Punjab Chief Minister Parkash Singh Badal today called upon various vice-chancellors of state universities and principals of the colleges to reserve at least 10 per cent seats for poor and bright rural students.

Addressing at a seminar on the book 'Gurmat Sabhayachar', authored by Sikh scholar and former SGPC president Kirpal Singh Badungar at the science auditorium in Punjabi University here today, Badal said the basic concept of Sikhism was to ensure equality in the society by removing the existing disparity between the rich and the poor. The Chief Minister also lauded the decision of the Centre to allow the state government to run short-term courses in skill development in schools and colleges after the working hours.

Heading: Heavy rain shatters 46-yr-old record - Indian Express
Content:
A team of Tarn Taran district health officials, acting on a tip-off, yesterday confiscated a truck containing 94 bags, each weighing 50 kilograms, of adulterated salt near the Amritsar by-pass. The consignment was coming from Rajasthan.

Tarn Taran Civil Surgeon Dr Amrit Kaur said the truck contained three brands of salt— Taza, Taj Mahal and Agni— and their samples were sent to Chandigarh for testing. As per the report, they were adulterated and contained little or no iodine, she said.

"Iodine is essential for pregnant women as its deficiency can lead to stillborn babies, mental retardation and lack of growth in children," she added.

Heading: Vehicles stranded in Lahaul valley - Indian Express
Content:
Several fallen deodars raise questions on illegal means of 'killing' trees

The recent unusual post-monsoon rain, which triggered heavy landslides and uprooted trees in Shimla, has broken the previous record of 1962 when the town witnessed the maximum rain. Yesterday, the town recorded 177.1 mm rain, exceeding the 158 mm recorded on September 21,1962.

City elders, however, recall that at that time only house collapse and landslides had occurred. But this time, the coming down of the majestic deodar trees — a few of them even two-centuries old — is being blamed on heavy construction activity and damage being caused to the trees by local residents.

Confirms Pankaj Khullar, Principal Chief Conservator of Forests: "Till now, more than 75 trees have already fallen, while 250 others have become a source of danger to the lives of local residents."

Sources said the committee, which was set up by the government to identify "dangerous" trees, has identified 415 trees for felling and provided photographs of 50 odd trees as supporting evidence.

On the other hand, it is common knowledge that some local residents, in order to clear the land of standing tree for taking up construction activities, adopt dangerous means to "kill" the trees or even dig out the roots and wait for the rains to bring them down. Ironically, the administration too does not have any policy to allow removing of these dangerous trees in time.

A religious organisation, which recently earned the wrath of the High Court, and also a few government agencies, beside locals, have been indulging in illegal methods to remove trees.

Reports from Jubbal-Kotkhai, Theog and Chopal belt — adversely affected by the landslides — confirm that dozens of green trees have fallen on the roads and the houses of people.

Heading: Declare new NHs: state to Centre - Indian Express
Content:
Adverse weather conditions have left more than 100 vehicles stranded between Baralacha Pass and Darcha in Lahaul valley, said C. Paul Rasu, Deputy Commissioner, Lahaul and Spiti, on Sunday. The DC said 100 big and small avalanches had occurred between Darcha and Baralacha Pass, adding that the district administration had provided blankets, ration and medicines to about 400 persons stranded on the road. Rasu said due to inclement weather conditions, helicopters could not join the rescue operation. "Leh administration has also joined hands with Kullu district in the clear-up operation," he said. The National Highway from Manali up to Rohtang Pass zero point was cleared of snow on Sunday, said Commander Doon of HQ 38 BRTF (GREF). He said the snow-clearing operation was still on. Sanjay Sharma, SHO, Manali, said though there was over four feet of snow at Rohtang Pass, all the stranded persons had been evacuated and the standard petrol tankers had been sent back to Marhi.

Rail, road traffic still hit in Solan

Landslides at several places caused suspension of railway and vehicular terrific for the second consecutive day on the Kalka-Shimla stretch and other internal roads of the district.

The worst-affected are the farmers, who are finding it difficult to transport their cash crops to various markets of the country. The railway authorities deputed labourers and small machines to clear the debris near Dharampur, Kumharhatti, Solan and other places, but continuous landslides is badly hampering the clearing operation. Health Minister Dr Rajeev Bindal said he had issued strict instructions to the officials concerned to initiate measures for immediate restoration of vehicular traffic on all major roads in rural parts of the district. Besides, instructions had also been issued to assess the loss caused by heavy downpour across the district.

Heading: Woman, 4 minor kids buried alive - Indian Express
Content: The Himachal Pradesh government has sent a fresh proposal to the Centre asking for declaring two new National Highways in view of growing economic activity and expansion of the road networks in the state. State's PWD Minister Gulab Singh Thakur, who was in Delhi recently, met the Minister for Shipping and Road Transport, T.R. Baalu, and submitted him a letter demanding that 91-km-long Nagrota-Ranital-Dehra-Mubarkpur road and 160 km Paonta-Rajban-Shillai-Meanus-Hatkoti road should be declared as national highways .

Heading: Himachal Confidential - Indian Express
Content:
Five members of a family, including four minor children, were buried alive in their house in Pain Kuffar village of Rajgarh tehsil in Sirmour district on Friday night following a landslide.

The rescue team — comprising a doctor, patwaris, veterinarian and police — which reached the spot on Saturday, retrieved the bodies with the help of locals. Gobind Ram, his father Jamia Ram and mother Kamla Devi, who received minor injuries, were given first-aid and treated. Gobind Ram's wife Savita and his four minor children, Ashu (4), Vikas (2), Shalu (6) and 3-month-old Gudu were among those who perished in the mishap.

SDM, Rajgarh, Rajesh Maria, when contacted on phone, said that Rs 25,000 had been given as immediate relief to the family and remaining ex-gratia amount of Rs 4.75 lakh would be given shortly. He said that loss of property and crop was being estimated for distributing compensation.

Maria said that a 50-metre-long stretch near Shalla Bag on Rajgarh-Shaila road had been washed away following a cloudburst, while Rajgarh had been cut off from other parts of the country.

"The Rajgarh-Minas-Solan road would be thrown open to traffic after removing the debris," he said. He said the farmers had suffered losses to the tune of lakhs of rupees because of the crop damage caused by the rains in the area.

Meanwhile, a 21-year-old man, a resident of Naraingarh in Haryana, was washed away in Markanda river, near Kala Amb, while he was crossing the river on Saturday.

* People vacate houses in panic

A number of residents of Harijan Basati in Chouras village had vacated their houses after big cracks developed in their houses. Mohan Lal, Pradhan of Nohradhar Panchayat, under Sangrah tehsil of Sirmour district, said continuous rain in the area had created havoc. He said that three mules of Joginder Pundir of Dev Mandal panchayat had been buried under the debris. Pundir also vacated his pucca house after it developed cracks. Mohan Lal said that a bridge had been washed away near Sautani and had been closed to traffic even as he had urged the district administration to get the road and bridge repaired at the earliest.

Heading: Eyes on Commonwealth Games 2010: Oscar - Indian Express
Content:
* Well spoken

When former MP Kripal Parmar was given a seat among the guests on the stage during an IT conferences in Shimla, the organisers of the programme announced him as a "sitting MP". Fearing any faux pas, they also invited him to the podium to address the audience. Though the MP announced that the call for him to speak had come as a surprise to him, "like I have been caught red-handed", his crisp and well-framed address proved that politicians are never really out of practice of public speaking.

* Name game

During Prem Kumar Dhumal's earlier tenure as Chief Minister, there were several officials by the last name of Katwal in the CMO. This time, it is the Dogras who are cause for confusion. Whenever the CM asks for calling up 'Dogra sahib', his secretary ponders for some time on who to call, as the Secretary (GAD and Personnel), Secretary (Law) and one Joint Secretary in the CM's Secretariat all go by the same name.

* Women rule

The BJP's announcement of giving 33 per cent reservation to women in the party seems to be getting implemented in the government, which has a big list of women bureaucrats. Some names are Chief Secretary Asha Swarup, Additional Chief Secretary Parminder Mathur, Tourism Secretary Manisha Nanda, who also holds charge of MD, Tourism, and CEO, Election Commission; Director, Health Services, Dr Sulakshana Puri and the latest to join the list — Director, Medical Education, Dr Jayshree Sharma.

* Rains hit shootings

The rains this year not only kept tourists away from Shimla, but also became a deterrent for film crews who usually prefer to shoot in Shimla during the summer. However, thinking that the weather would improve in September, many producers had lined up for shooting in Shimla, but the sudden bad weather has delayed many projects, including Vidhu Vinod Chopra's Aamir Khan-starrer "Idiot".

Heading: Buddha's plea: End stir or else Tatas will leave Bengal - Indian Express
Content:
After having walked away with the Player of the Tournament by winning four titles in the 19th Yonex Chandigarh State Open Badminton Championship, international shuttler Oscar Bansal hopes to repeat his performance this year also. "I am in good form now and hopefully, I will be able to repeat last year's performance in the championship," says the student of Bachelor of Engineering in Electronics and Communication in Panjab University. "But right now I am concentrating on the North Zone Championship to be held at Amritsar," adds Bansal.

After a roller-coaster ride during the past year, Oscar has come a long way. Having blossomed into a fine shuttler, he has graduated to the senior circuit from the junior level. "The transition of a player from junior to senior is quite hard to adjust. There is hardly any competition at the junior level but in the senior circuit you have to be a versatile player and know the game and playing style of your opponent," says the 19-year-old shuttler who has represented India in Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand and Czech Republic.

The 36 days coaching camp from June 14 to July 20 at Bangalore has worked wonders for him. "It was an enriching experience. All the top ranked Indian shuttlers of the likes of Anup Aridhar and Anand Bhatt were present there. I played few games against them and managed to surpsise them with my game. Even the coach present there praised my game. My fitness level has improved a lot from the camp since a lot of emphasis was being given on physical training at the camp apart from coaching," says the bespectacled Oscar who started playing the game when he was 11 years old.

Oscar is currently looking forward to the Commonwealth Games 2010.

"Our coach Gopichand will hold camps for about 20-25 days and after that he will select the players. I have attended the camps in Hyderabad for two-three times. Hopefully I will play in the Commonwealth Games but my ultimate goal is to play for the Olympics. I have kept that goal in mind and I am working hard to improve my game," says the shuttler who recently participated in the Panjab University Badminton Inter-college tournament.

Heading: CITU defers strike after HPL management seeks time - Indian Express
Content:
Making a fresh appeal to the Opposition parties to stop their agitation at Singur, Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee on Sunday warned that the Tatas would leave West Bengal if they are not allowed to resume work soon.

"I appeal to all the Opposition parties of the state to accept the package the Government has announced for the farmers in Singur (and) withdraw all agitational programmes," said Bhattacharjee in his statement.

"If there is further delay, this project will go out of the state. So without any delay, let the Tatas and the ancillary units come back and resume work in a peaceful manner. Let all of us unite and take the initiative of implementing the project in the interest of not only the people of Singur but the people of West Bengal as a whole and also future generations," he said.

Minister for External Affairs Pranab Mukherjee, who was in Baharampur on Sunday, also warned that if the state lost the project, it would hamper industrialisation. "If the Tatas pull out, it will be very unfortunate. It will give a big jolt to the process of industrialisation in the state," he said.

However, Trinamool Congress leader Mamata Banerjee turned down the Chief Minister's appeal and said her party was giving a week's time to the state government to return 300 acres of land from the project site.

"The state government flouted the agreement that was reached in front of Governor Gopalkrishna Gandhi," said Banerjee.

"We are giving seven days time to implement this agreement. Meanwhile, we will go to the Governor, Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and President Pratibha Patil, requesting them to intervene in the matter. We will also urge the Central government to dismiss the state government because it broke all democratic norms and traditions," she said at the end of a meeting of the Krishijomi Rakka Committee at Trinamool Bhavan.

Meanwhile, in Singur two more cheques were handed out, taking the total number of farmers who received compensation to 27.

The number of applications for cheques now stands at 45.

The deadline for giving 10 per cent of the compensation money to all those who did not receive cheques is expiring on Monday.

Heading: Kolkata confidential - Indian Express
Content:
Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU), CPM's labour wing, has decided to defer its three-day strike at the Haldia Petrochemicals Limited plant in East Midnapore.

The strike was to come into effect from September 22. The union is demanding, among other things, the regularisation of 183 casual employees working at the plant since 2000.

Haldia CITU leader Ashok Patanaik said they decided to defer the strike after they received a letter sent by the HPL management on Sunday afternoon. Through the letter, the management asked for a few days time to sort out the issue of regularisation of the employees. Patanaik said, "We are ready to resolve the issues through talks. We are ready to give time to the management." He, however, warned that the strike cannot be deferred indefinitely.

Heading: Compost plant lying waste, KMC fails to keep contract - Indian Express
Content:
Singur solution?

The aftershocks of the Big Bang experiment at Switzerland last week had been felt at the Writers' too, with ministers, including Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee, curious to know what it was all about. Principal secretaries sat glued to television sets in their cabins. Other employees were seen huddled in corridors, busy discussing if and when the apocalypse will strike. "The state government would not mind an apocalypse now. There will be no Singur to handle," said an official, tongue firmly in cheek.

'Speak no evil'

Last week, Dilip Chakrabarty, Principal Secretary of the Department of Information and Culture, was taken aback when veteran actor Soumitra Chatterjee came as part of the delegation to meet him about the handing over of Technicians' Studio to Zee Telefilms. But it was not a pleasant surprise that the civil servant had. As the delegation, including filmmakers Rituparno Ghosh and Gautam Ghosh, actors Prasenjit and Jeet, launched into a criticism of the government for handing over the studio to a private concern, Chakrabarty pleaded it had all been discussed with Soumitrababu, who was sitting right there. But no solace was forthcoming from that quarter. Instead of backing him up, Chatterjee sat mum throughout the meeting.

Toting up the numbers

The contest to win over the disposed farmers in Singur is turning into a numbers game, say workers of both CPM and the Trinamool Congress. At the offices of both parties, the talk these days is not about whether the Tatas will stay back or if the government will agree to give back more land. Rather, it's about how many farmers would be taken to the Singur DM's office to either accept cheques or demand their land back. Post-dharna, several farmers have "deserted" the Mamata camp and accepted the money they were refusing so far. Others have offered to "return" the money they have already accepted and are asking for their land back.

Safety first

Where can you hide inside a high security prison? This was the question the jail officers and guards of Presidency Central Jail were asking on September 16. For two hours, those same officers were held at ransom by a group of inmates, who were protesting against the transfer of a ganglord. When the protest began — around 3.30 pm — the "trained" officers and guards ran looking for a place to hide: the bathroom, under tables and behind filing cabinets. This went on till reinforcements arrived. Later, the state jail minister, Biswanath Choudhury, had to request Chief Minister Buddadeb Bhattacharjee for a special force for such emergencies.

JU upgrades itself

The fact that the Jadavpur University offices have gone for a major facelift and the unprecedented decision of suspending 24 students for ragging may not be just another amusing coincidence. The JU administrative offices have received a complete "corporate" makeover, with swanky new flooring, fancy gates, elegant curtains and plush sofa sets at the lobbies. Asked about the new look, a senior faculty member of the university chuckled, "yes, the look is 'corporate' and so is the penalty — quite stringent". He was, of course, referring to the university's decision to suspend 24 students in the ragging case.

Coaching blues

As the Ranji Trophy approaches, the Bengal cricket administration could have done better than to merely put together a huge, unmanageable band of nearly 50 probable players for coaches to handle. Coaches Mohinder Amarnath and Utpal Chatterjee, exasperated with the CAB's policy, finally took the call themselves to save the situation, slicing off the unwanted 'half' from the total pool, and pruning the list of probables down to the men who matter.

Heading: Kidney racket busted, 1 arrested - Indian Express
Content:
A Rs 7 crore compost plant, set up by Eastern Organic Fertilizer Pvt Ltd, has been caught in a legal tangle between the company and the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) over the issue of supply of raw material for the plant. The plant was shut down in 2004 and hopes of resumption of work are minimal.

During the tenure of Mayor Prashanta Chatterjee in 1994, the civic body had signed an agreement with Excel Industries Pvt Ltd, Mumbai. According to the agreement, 30 acres of land was leased out to the company that later sub-leased the land to Eastern Organic Fertilizer Pvt Ltd after taking permission from the KMC.

The plant was inaugurated in 2000 during the tenure of Mayor Subrata Mukherjee. Initially, the plant was running smoothly but soon it started facing operational problems since it was not receiving soft garbage, which the civic body was required to supply under the 1994 agreement.

The civic authorities, however, said the company has violated two major clauses of the agreement.

Arun Sarkar, Chief Municipal Engineer( Solid Waste Management Department), said: "Initially, the company told us that the plant would consume 700 metric tonnes of garbage for making compost. Further, the company is required to give us a certain amount of revenue."

He alleged, "Since its set up in 2000, the company has been defaulting on revenue. Moreover, it never took 700 metric tons of waste."

For manufacturing compost, a plant needs either food-waste or organic waste as raw material. The company officials had asked the KMC to supply flower, fruit and vegetable waste. The company's counsel Jayanta Mitro said: "According to the contract, the KMC is supposed to supply soft waste but it provided concrete waste that is not suited for making compost."

He refuted the charges of not paying the revenue. "The waste material damaged the company's machines. Even then we never defaulted on revenue. We even tried to collect the suitable waste from outside to keep the plant functional but the civic body did not let us do that and forced us to shut down the plant," said Mitro.

He claimed that the KMC had broken the agreement.

Officials of the solid waste management department, however, have a different take. "We do not have waste segregation system. So the company has to accept the waste that we supply," said an official.

A senior civic official admitted that the KMC had failed to fulfill its obligations under the contract. "The KMC did not provide the waste material. Consequently, the company was not able to extract compost from the waste that consists of bricks, cement and other concrete pieces," he added.

Following the non-availability of raw material, the compost plant was shut down in 2004.

The company initiated legal proceedings after all efforts of mutual agreement with the KMC had failed. A hearing in the case is going on in the High Court.

It has also affected work on KMC's projects, including the construction of the sanitary landfill site and the "waste to electricity" project. "KMC cannot take its land back since the clauses of the agreement are not only violated by the company but by KMC also," said a civic official.

Heading: Funds for food lab lie idle, KMC least concerned - Indian Express
Content:
North Dinajpur police busted a kidney trafficking racket and arrested the alleged mastermind from Bindal near Raiganj on Saturday night. Abdul Razzaq was produced in the Raiganj court on Sunday morning and was remanded in judicial custody for 14 days.

Razzaq, a resident of Antara village in Bindal, is suspected of having duped Bindal villagers and stolen their kidneys with the help of doctors in New Delhi, Mumbai and Kolkata.

Inspector-in-charge of Raiganj police station, Pradip Chakraborty said: "After Razzaq's arrest, some of his victims approached us and informed about the racket."

A Bindal resident, Chottu Murmu lodged an FIR with the Raiganj police on Sunday evening. It stated that Razzaq had taken him to Kolkata in September 2007 for treatment. He got him admitted to a city hospital, where he was operated upon. Murmu later came to know that his kidney had been removed.

Police said Razzaq has confessed of having stolen kidneys of over 30 people. He would lure people with a promise of providing jobs in metros and then get them admitted to a hospital where they would be operated upon, said police.

The police said Razzaq confessed to running the racket in Kolkata for the last four years. "He had forged connections with hospitals like Woodlands, Bellevue, Apollo and the government-run SSKM," said a police officer.

His network was spread across North and South Dinajpur, Malda and Bihar.

Heading: GJM mollified after talks with Centre, may scale down ops - Indian Express
Content:
A fund of Rs 1.2 crore for an upgraded food laboratory of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), sanctioned by the Central Food Processing Department (CFPD) two years ago, lies unused as KMC is yet to prepare a Detailed Project Report (DPR).

Considering that the food laboratory was not equipped to test pesticides and metal residues in foods and beverages, the civic body had

approached the CFPD for funds for upgrading the lab in 2006. The CFPD had then asked for a project report. The civic authorities, however, are yet to finalise a place to shift the laboratory. It was earlier decided that the premises of the existing lab, the Hogg Street Building, would be extended to house the new one.

The KMC, however, could not carry it out because of the heritage status of the Hogg Street Building. Later, the civic body found a place at Kalighat but that was also rejected because the place was quite far from the KMC head office. Now, the KMC is considering setting up the lab in the Indian Medical Association (IMA) building at Park Circus.

The funds sanctioned, however, are on the verge of being declared unusable due to the unprecedented delay in executing the project.

"The higher authorities are yet to prepare the DPR," said a health official of the KMC.

Joint Commissioner (KMC) Sahidul Islam seemed indifferent to the prospect of expiry of the CFPD funds.

"If we cannot use the fund sanctioned by the CFPD, then we can use the grant given by Department for International Development for the upgradation of the food laboratory," he said.

Debdwaipayan Chattopadhyay, Chief Medical Health Official of the civic body, denied the entire issue. "The CFPD has not sanctioned any fund. We are proceeding with the project on our own resources," he said.

Heading: Land acquisition blues continue for Left Front, now in Siliguri - Indian Express
Content:
Following the first round of tripartite talks in New Delhi, the Gorkha Janamukti Morcha (GJM) has indicated that it could scale down its ongoing "non-cooperation movement" in the Darjeeling Hills.

Senior GJM leader Amar Lama told The Indian Express that the first round of talks had lent them confidence that their demands will be considered by the Central government.

"Though the West Bengal government has ruled out any possibility of a separate Gorkhaland, the matter is now with the Centre. Their response during the talks (on September 8) was good, so we want to create an atmosphere conducive to talks," Lama said. To facilitate this, the GJM is planning to relax the non-cooperation movement.

The areas of the movement to be reviewed is to be decided at a meeting later this week, he said. "We have met the Union home secretary and submitted a booklet explaining our stand and case history. We have also explained why we don't want to enter into talks with the Bengal government. The Centre has said they will meet us again in November for the next round of talks," Lama said.

Launched in June, the movement has reduced government revenue to a trickle, as the GJM has issued a diktat forbidding residents to pay taxes, telephone and electricity bills.

"The Motor Vehicles Department is losing nearly Rs 45 lakh per month by way of unpaid road tax and registration fees. The Land Reforms department is suffering losses of around Rs 1 crore as no one is paying land taxes, including property tax. The electricity department is also earning Rs 1.5 crore less than usual. The lotteries have been closed down," said a source.

Lama, however, indicated that there will be no turning back from enforcing the conversion of vehicle number plates from West Bengal (WB) to Gorkhaland (GL). Since the first week of July, number plates have been changed phasewise in the Hills. At present, most private vehicles in Darjeeling town sport GL plates painted with the GJM's colours — green and yellow. "Now, number plates of taxis will also be converted," Lama said.

Official vehicles, too, are under the GJM diktat. The district administration, however, said they have found a way to beat the number plate conversion. Darjeeling District Magistrate Surendra Gupta said while his vehicle along with the SP's, SDOs and the judiciary are bearing WB plates, junior employees are using hired vehicles. "Our main concern is to maintain law and order. By using taxis, we are complying indirectly with the GJM's demand while ensuring that the plates of government vehicles remain unchanged," Gupta added.

Heading: Eviction at Great Eastern? Government turns a deaf ear - Indian Express
Content:
The ghost of land acquisition is haunting the Left Front government again. Its coalition partner Revolutionary Socialist Party (RSP) has taken up the cudgels on behalf of people whose land was acquired by the government nearly two years ago for setting up a satellite township project in Siliguri.

The RSP has joined hands with the Congress and the Trinamool Congress in opposing the land acquisition. The party's Darjeeling district secretary Benoy Chakraborty said: "The government should not force people to give up their land. It should

also make public all details of the compensation package and the township blueprint through gazette notifications."

The state government, through the Siliguri Jalpaiguri Development Authority (SJDA), seeks to acquire 320 acres for the project, of which it alraedy has nearly 270 acres. Landowners of 50-odd acres have refused to give up their holdings and have approached the Calcutta High Court against the acquisition drive.

Interestingly, those who have accepted the compensation are now protesting under the banner of the Bhumi Raksha Samiti, earlier led by veteran Naxalite leader Kanu Sanyal, but now led by West Bengal Pradesh Congress Committee secretary Deepa Dasmunsi. The landowners have also formed a group, the Kawakhali Landowners' Association (KLA).

Chakraborty said: "The KLA has asked me to take up their cause. The compensation package came up for discussion during the LF meeting on Thursday, where it was decided that the package would be endorsed only if the dispossessed landowners approved it." He further added, "We met

Urban Development Minister Ashok Bhattacharya. He will take up our case at the next meeting of the Front." He alleged that the government is acting like a broker, acquiring land at cheaper rates and selling it to developers. This is similar to the Singur situation, he said.

Deepa Dasmunsi said the compensation package failed to meet the promises made by the government. "Of the 1,400 farmers who lost their land, 598 did not receive any benefit. They want their land back. Most of them are poor people holding marginal land," she added.

"Bhattacharya had convinced the landowners to give up their land at a nominal cost of only Rs 8,000-22,000 per cottah. He promised several benefits to them but nothing has come as yet," said the Congress leader.

Bhattacharya, however, has expressed surprise over the protests and said the compensation package was one of the best in the country.

The SJDA is acquiring land at Kawakhali, Purajhar and Tikulikatha villages near the North Bengal Medical College and Hospital in Siliguri, to facilitate the establishment of a satellite township by Bengal Universal Unitech.

Heading: Presidency jail violence costs one more life - Indian Express
Content:
Singed by its experience at Singur and Nandigram, the state government has refused to intervene even after the Great Eastern Hotel — unable to evict its three remaining tenants — has sought the help of Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee.

The hotel had 44 tenants when the state government went for a joint venture with Delhi-based Bharat Hotels Ltd, which had shelled out Rs 52 crore.

Of the 44, only three — Blue Print, a medicine shop, Newmans', a garments shop, and Singer India Ltd which has its office here — have refused to vacate the premises. They claim that are not getting adequate compensation.

The hotel authorities had sought the chief minister's help them in the matter but the state government has flatly refused.

"Why should we intervene? It's something between Great Eastern Hotel and the three tenants. The government does not want to get involved in this," Sumanta Choudhury, Principal Secretary, Department of Public Sector Undertakings, told The Indian Express. The state government has a 10 per cent share in the hotel.

The Blue Print has threatened to take the help of Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee if the state government intervenes in the matter. "I am ready to go and do not want to stand in the way of building the hotel," said Milon Roy of Blue Print. "I am not asking for the moon. I am asking for the money which will be commensurate with the market rate. If I get that money, I will start my business afresh."

The work at the hotel, meanwhile, is going on in full swing. The hotel authorities say it will open for public by the end of next year.

Heading: Too many rhinos? Straying incidents leave experts baffled - Indian Express
Content:
Another inmate of the Presidency Central Jail, Muhammed Jehangir, died at the SSKM Hospital on Sunday. His relatives staged a protest inside the hospital, alleging that he was thrashed by the jail officials during the Tuesday's violence inside the jail premises.

DIG (Jail) S R Hussain said: "Jehangir was suffering from tuberculosis. The cause of death will be known after the postmortem report."

On Wednesday, Muhhamed Azharuddin, an undertrial of the Presidency Central Jail, had succumbed to his injuries in the jail. Both Jehangir and Azharuddin were injured in a clash with the prison guards on Tuesday, when they and other jailbirds were resisting the transfer of gangster Zafar Siddiqui alias Gudda from the jail.

Jehangir was admitted to the SSKM hospital on Saturday after he complained of severe chest pain and breathlessness. One of his relatives said: "The jail officials had thrashed him badly on Tuesday. He had immediately complained of chest pain and nausea. Blood was oozing from his mouth but the jail staff paid no heed."

Jehangir , he said, was admitted to the hospital when his condition became critical on Saturday. "He died due to negligence and high-handedness of the jail authorities," he added.

The jail officials, however, claimed that he was suffering from acute tuberculosis and had been admitted to the M R Bangur hospital twice for treatment. They also said he had sustained only minor injuries during Tuesday's violence. The SSKM authorities said he was a TB patient and was suffering from severe pneumonia.

Jehangir, a resident of Taltolla, was arrested on charges of dacoity and possession of illegal arms in 2006.

Nearly 40 prisoners, all aides of city-based mafia don Gudda, had attacked the prison guards with blades and bricks on Tuesday afternoon, when they were trying to transfer him to the Dum Dum Central Jail. The guards, in turn, retaliated with with batons.

The state jail department has already ordered a high-level inquiry into the incident and the deaths.

Heading: Mamata trains guns at govt on Rehman’s death anniversary - Indian Express
Content:
Two rhinos that strayed into human habitation in north Bengal were driven back in the forest area on Sunday. A 10-year-old female rhino and its five-year-old calf had strayed out from the Gorumara National Park on Friday night.

Divisional Forest Officer Tapas Das said, "Forty officials of the Wild Life wing, along with two kunki (trained) elephants, were pressed into action to push the mother-calf duo into forests."

This is the second case of rhinos straying in less than a week. A male adult rhino had strayed from the core area of the Gorumara park on September 15 and went marauding through five villages in Mainaguri block of Jalpaiguri.

Recurrence of such incidents has left wildlife experts baffled. Though Friday's incident is cited as a "stray" incident, Bengal's success story in rhino conservation could have a host of adverse fall-outs.

The number of rhinoceros in Jaldapara Wildlife Sanctuary has increased from 14 to 122 in the last 21 years. This is a welcome departure from the days when the rhino population had come down to 12 in Jaldapara and six in the Gorumara National Park.

In 1986, the number of one-horned rhinoceros in Jaldapara was 14, which went up to 108 exactly two decades later.

Gorumara now has a rhino population of 30.

The straying could be an indicator that the rhinoceros population in Jaldapara and Gorumara has reached the threshold limit of the carrying capacity of the area.

"As of now, it still seems to be just within the limit. But an ever-increasing rhino population could trigger an ecological imbalance. There could be more strayings leading to man-rhino conflict which until now remain unheard of," said Colonel Shakti Banerjee, Honorary Director, Wildlife Protection Society of India.

It has also led to the skewed male-female ratio of the rhino population. While the ideal ratio is one male for every two females, in Gorumara, it is one male for each female, leading to infighting among the animals.

Heading: Beat It - Indian Express
Content:
Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee occupied the centre stage, as she led a rally demanding justice for Rizwanur Rehman, on the occasion of his first death anniversary on Sunday.

The rally that snaked through the streets of Park Circus saw a large turnout with locals carrying banners and placards.

Rehman's brother Rukbanur said a year had passed by since Rehman was found murdered but there has been no headway in the case.

He, however, added that his family was hopeful that justice would now be done since the HC had asked the CBI to chargesheet the accused and take up further investigations.

"We hope for justice. Didi (Mamata) is with us. She has been very supportive since the beginning. We all remember Rehman and miss him greatly. We want that his killers be brought to book. We hope the CBI investigation will bring out the truth ," Rukbanur said.

Claiming that Rehman was murdered, Banerjee said: "The guilty must be punished and the corrupt political establishment that encourages such crimes needs to be uprooted."

She blamed the state government for the delay in justice and said: "One week after Rehman's death, Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee had assured his family that justice would be delivered. But his government has only tried to protect the accused."

She claimed that thousands of people in the state are waiting for justice but the process was being delayed.

Banerjee added that a health clinic and a computer training centre would be opened in the area in Rehman's memory.

Heading: Vision for the Wilderness - Indian Express
Content:
That's what a group of professionals in the city is saying to gender violence, having launched a campaign after the Juhu molestation

SHE walks hurriedly past the throng of people coming her way. All she wants is to reach her destination on time. From the corner of a lane, he waits patiently to ruin her day; a look, a word or a gesture will do the job, he knows. Then, in a flash, they are side by side, he pinches her lightly and moves on. But she turns back with surprising nerve, she will not take this lying down; she will fight back.

A quick look around crowded places in Mumbai is enough to agree that thousands of women endure such harassment on a daily basis. And also to see that only a few will take action.

With that in mind, comprehending the problems victims face in coming out in the open to speak up against gender violence, a group of twenty-somethings who work at a media organization in Central Mumbai decided to create a platform for such women. And that's how Fight-back was created, spurred into action by the New Year's eve incident at Juhu.

"We have heard about rape, eve-teasing, groping incidents. But the Juhu molestation case was a true eye-opener. We had noticed that when any such heinous act comes to light, it makes front page news for a couple of days, the stake holders come into the picture, and the case goes on for some days before it all goes dead. People forget about the incident till the next victim grabs headlines," says Sonali Hans (34), one of the members.

The group was formed primarily by 38-year-old Zubin Driver, a media professional who was irked by gender violence and decided to bring his friends together.

The core team of Fight-back comprises 10 people. Interestingly, six are male.

"We feel very strongly about gender violence, there is no question of male chauvinism when dealing with it. Most of my female friends and colleagues have complained of being eve-teased or molested at least once. I am sure that is the case with most women in the country. What makes the situation worse is that for most of them this has become a way of life and they just turn a blind eye," says Siddhartha Aneja (24).

As a start, group has manufactured special wallet cards bearing the telephone numbers of all police stations in the city. "Before starting the group, we consulted the Mumbai police who readily supported the cause; we ensured that all the numbers we are printing are actually operational," says Hans. "We also consulted lawyers who readily agreed to help us, pro-bono. Often, victims don't know what legal action to take, the cards will give them a ready option to consult experts and proceed," Hans adds.

The cards have been distributed to women at various public places like railway stations, bus stops, schools and colleges.

To catch the attention of youngsters, the group has also tied up with organizers of events like rock concerts and the Mumbai Marathon. "I-rock concert has been a big boost for us, music cuts across barriers. We used the platform to sensitize the youth about gender violence," says Aarthi Gunnunuri (23), another member. They have also started a community on social networking site Facebook to spread the message. In addition to this, the group has its own website www.fightback.net.

Next on the agenda is to take the campaign to rural areas. "Though it is a low key movement, we have got tremendous response from the urban areas. But, rural areas still remain a problem; and gender violence there is even more severe," says Aneja, on the challenges before them in making this a "truly pan-India movement".

Heading: A newspaper cutting for every malady - Indian Express
Content:
The Wilson College Nature Club that had its annual reunion recently is among the city's most active groups of adventure lovers and eco-warriors

THIS group comprises an assortment of people- students, ex-students, teachers and professionals, with a wide gap in their ages and backgrounds. But what unites the motley bunch that makes up the Wilson College Nature Club, however, is an undying love of adventure and the outdoors.

Twenty-nine years since its inception, the WCNC, as it is popularly known, is one of the oldest active nature clubs in the city, and a reunion held on Saturday was attended by many. "We started out by going and meeting all the teachers in the college, but only one professor, Baldev Vakharia, actually took the initiative to help set up the nature club.

In our first year, we were nine members, in our second, 110, and in our third year the number rose to 300," recalls Farhan Thakur, one of the founder-members of the WCNC, and chairperson of the club in 1979-1980.

"In the beginning, the emphasis on the trails was more on plants. Later, it diversified into much more," says founder-member Shripath Kabe. "We went on a World Wildlife Fund (WWF) camp as volunteers and got into bird-watching. Soon, we each had our areas of interest — Farhan's was butterflies and birds, and Kabe's was plants. The best thing about the Nature Club is that it helps you learn a variety of skills," adds Mahmood Kadri, another founder member.

Known for its treks, the WCNC regularly hosts camps, nature trails and annual exhibitions. "For our first exhibition, we borrowed a large collection of birds from a taxidermist friend, Oswald Thayil. We took a tree from the grounds of the college, put it on stage and recreated a forest," says Thakur. The WCNC exhibitions focus on the issues of the hour, and cover a variety of topics.

"This year, the topic is 'Natural Habitats and the Hippo Effect' and the exhibition is scheduled for November. To get more people involved, we have started a mailing list to inform them about the activities of the nature club. Anyone who wants to become a member just has to contact us at Wilson College," says Disha Pinge, a student of mass media.

Stories of strange and alarming incidents on previous camps have become the stuff of lore among members. "On a camp in Himachal Pradesh, we were stuck on a mountain-top, with wind-chills of minus three blowing around. The mules carrying our bags had lost their way, so we didn't have any warm clothes either," recalls WCNC member

Gayathri Bhaskaran. "On a trip to Ladakh, we were stuck in a snowstorm at Khardung-La, the highest motorable pass in the world, and we had to melt ice for water since all the water we had was frozen. Thirty-five of us shared a few bars of chocolate, since we had no other food," recollects Glen D'Souza, another member. The WCNC has also made it a point to do regular clean-ups, workshops and tree-plantation drives, and walked away with the Best Team award at a clean-up drive held recently at the Sanjay Gandhi National Park.

"The main thing about the club is that students can do things that they otherwise wouldn't have the opportunity to do, and the rates for the treks are more subsidized than others available. No matter what the difference in age, there is a sense of community when one is a member of the Nature Club," says Sudhakar Solomonraj, staff advisor and the main force behind the WCNC. The next trip planned is a twelve day trip to Annamalai in November, something that has all the members involved gearing up for, ready to rough it out and have fun, WCNC style.

Heading: Renewed bid to get green clearance for Peddar Rd flyover - Indian Express
Content:
Ghatkopar's Police Inspector Fulsingh Pawar has a treasure trove of 8,000 cuttings. He dips in each time a dispute wanders into his office

Be it a wife's repeated grouse about her husband's poor financial status or a brawl between two slum-dwellers, a policeman at the Ghatkopar police station has found a unique tool to unravel discordant strings and negotiate a truce.

Police Inspector Fulsingh Pawar, whose brief is to handle community issues, says he has had tremendous success with such incidents that end at his police station every day, whether they are warring couples, juvenile delinquents or local trouble-makers. And they all visit Pawar expecting a long sermon but find themselves reading newspaper articles on various issues relevant to their dispute. And every cutting is selected from the 49-year-old Pawar's large, and still growing, collection of newspaper cuttings.

Pawar possesses a collection of over 8,000 newspaper cuttings, prominent columns and other inspirational news stories dating as far back as the early 1980s. While the ones he uses as part of his counseling activities at work are neatly pasted into thick, hard-bound journals for easy viewing, the other cuttings are filed away neatly, ready reference material when he delivers lectures on various topics.

"If I have to counsel a couple on 'adjustment', I focus on a story which speaks about that. If a youth has been nabbed for some crime, I refer to news reports that explain how innocent citizens bear the brunt of someone else's selfish decision. These articles make the counseling process interesting and the message is conveyed in an unforgettable way" says Pawar.

"Reading has been a passion since childhood and reading newspapers has been a fixation," says Pawar, who still reads 17 newspapers in English, Hindi and Marathi every day. While several cuttings of columns by management gurus like Robin Sharma and Vijay Batra adorn his journal, the policeman also stresses that he possesses every article from the 'India Empowered' series by The Indian Express that ran in 2005-2006.

With over 600 books, 30 journals and umpteen files adding up to his collection, Pawar admits that the lack of space is a great obstacle. "I live in alone in a small police quarter while my 60-member joint family stays in Solapur. My home can hardly encompass all the collected material, so most of my books are at my friend's residence," he explains.

It is his solitary life in Mumbai that permits him to work over 18 hours a day, he says. "Very few families would permit a member to devote so much time to work. However, I consider myself a social worker first and a policeman later and while I have been a policeman for 25 years now, I have been working for the community for longer," says Pawar. He then lists four factors he considers key at his counseling sessions: "Hospitality, a sweet but true tongue, empathy and a smile. These are never forgotten," he says.

A network engineer and one of Pawar's success stories, Prashant Sable, refers to Pawar as a godsend, even holding him as the sole reason for the success of his marriage. "My wife, an advocate by profession, and I were separated for around a year as she was not willing to stay in a chawl. However Pawar gave her a cutting of the story of Mandakini Amte, who chose to accompany her husband into a forest to serve people. Now there is no turmoil in our marriage," he says.

Heading: Soon, seven rly stations to get escalators - Indian Express
Content:
After failing to get environmental clearance for the city's most controversial flyover proposed on Peddar Road, the Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation (MSRDC) has gone back to the Maharashtra Coastal Zone Management Authority requesting, once again, that permission be granted for the viaduct design that involves two piers right on Girgaum Chowpatty.

In July, a committee had rejected the MSRDC's design of the proposed flyover, which currently juts seven metres into the beach and pegs two pillars on Chowpatty, sending the plan back to the drawing board eight years after it was mooted.

The MCZMA, the state agency that oversees all coastal construction activities, had rejected permission to the flyover on similar grounds in 2006 as well. However, MSRDC still went ahead and wrote to the MCZMA, appealing for approval saying it was unable to redesign the section that intrudes onto the beach.

"We have written to the MCZMA to allow MSRDC to continue with the design of the two piers on Chowpatty," confirmed Anil Deshmukh, Public Works Department minister. The MCZMA had in its meeting decided that if the MSRDC could not make changes due to technical reasons it could come back to the committee for clearance, he added.

With the Bandra-Worli Sea Link nearing completion, a decision on a traffic dispersal system — either a tunnel linking its Worli end with Marine Drive or the Peddar Road flyover — has become doubly urgent, traffic experts say . According to the minister, the proposed acute bend at Chowpatty is expected to reduce the speed of vehicular traffic, while bending it further would "considerably" bring down the speed that may result in major bottlenecks in future. "The current curve at Chowpatty with two piers on the beach brings down the average speed to around 35 kmph. If the curve is sharper we expect the average speed to come down to around 12 kmph, which could cause major jams in future," Deshmukh explained.

Now the fate of the Rs 135-crore flyover, which has been a non-starter since 2000, lies once again with the MCZMA. Apart from the environmental clearance, the project has also faced opposition from local residents including singers Lata Mangeshkar and Asha Bhosale, both of whom live on Peddar Road.

Heading: Caught at airport: NRI ferrying 100 kg of drugs to Mexico - Indian Express
Content:
Proposal aimed at easing commuting for disabled and senior citizens, announced in Rail Budget this year, now gets Railway Board sanction

Suburban railway stations in the financial capital will soon offer a facility now common in airports and malls across the country, but unheard of at railway stations ¿ escalators.

The Railway Board has sanctioned escalators for seven stations — four for Western Railway and three at Central Railway stations ¿ on a trial basis. Apart from this, three lifts will also be installed by December at Platform Numbers 16, 17 and 18 of the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, on the foot overbridge connecting the new station complex to the to old terminus.

The idea of installing escalators had been discussed in the year's railway budget too and officials are now tying up plans on which stations will be shortlisted.

The four WR stations that will get escalators are Virar, Borivali, Andheri and Dadar. Each station will have two escalator pairs, one each at the eastern and western entrance. The total cost of these eight escalators is estimated at Rs 5 crore.

"Very soon, tenders will be floated. The entire procedure from tendering up to awarding the contract and installing the escalators will take at least a year," said a senior WR official.

WR has also chalked in safety features into the plan. Chief Public Relations Officer (WR) Shyam Sunder Gupta said: "Till now, injuries have occurred on stair-type escalators. WR is considering the ramp-type escalators." However, he admitted that fewer companies manufacture such escalators.

On Central Railway, the stations selected for installing escalators are Kalyan, Thane and Dadar, six escalator pairs at a total cost of Rs 3.75 crore.

"The proposal has been sent to the Railway Board," confirmed Chief Public Relations Officer (CR) S Mudgerikar. "It will be beneficial for people, especially for the physically challenged, senior citizens, pregnant women and others."

Apart from this, three lifts have been planned for the Foot Over Bridge connecting CST to the P D'Mello Road entrance to the new extension for outstation trains. While the FOB is nearly complete, empty spaces have been left for installing these lifts. "By December this year you should see these lifts being placed here," said Mudgerikar.

Heading: For firemen, burning issues remain health insurance and risk allowance - Indian Express
Content:
Officers of the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) arrested a Canada-based non-resident Indian and a clearing agent from Mumbai early Sunday morning for allegedly trying to send 100 kg of contraband Ephedrine tablets to Mexico. NCB sleuths said the contraband is worth over Rs 1.5 crore in the international market.

According to the officials, they received a tip-off acting on which a team of NCB sleuths raided the cargo of a Mexico-bound flight at Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport and seized the contraband. "Ephedrine is used to make Ecstasy pills. Ephedrine is a major component in preparing banned drugs like Ecstasy and Ice that are consumed in parties worldwide. These drugs are banned not only in the US and Canada but also in India," said an official of the NCB.

Manprit Bal, the NRI based in Canada, was arrested around 4 am on Sunday along with his alleged accomplice, an Indian clearing and forwarding agent identified only as Ajay S. "We had information that a huge quantity of Ephedrine is being sent in a consignment to Mexico. Accordingly we scanned the cargo and seized the contraband. We arrested Bal from a hotel in Mumbai. He had come down to India to arrange to send the consignment," the official added.

According to the officer, there is an international mafia that smuggles Ephedrine to Mexico. There are several other Canadians on the NCB radar who are presently on the run, the official said.

Meanwhile, on Saturday, the NCB also arrested an alleged international drug dealer with an Interpol red corner notice against him. David Dominic was nabbed at the Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport (CSIA) while on his way out of the country. According to an airport source, Dominic was bound for Dubai. Senior Police Inspector Dilip Patil of Sahar Police Station said Dominic had been arrested in the United States in 2005 but had jumped bail, causing the red corner notice to be issued in his name. He may have been in India since.

"Dominic was arrested and produced before a holiday court this afternoon in Bandra and has been remanded to police custody," Patil added. According to an airport official, no contraband was found on him.

"Dominic will eventually be handed over to the CBI in New Delhi from where the extradition process will begin," Patil added.

Heading: In Marathi and about Maharashtra, Tingya will go to Oscars as independent entry - Indian Express
Content:
Civic administration to issue them smart cards to ensure medical benefits including hospitalisation without a deposit fee

Kavita Sangrulkar doesn't believe that a fireman's job is quite as exciting as depicted in fiction or in superhero accounts. Her cynicism is not misdirected: Her brother Abhay Mohite, a fireman working with the Mumbai Fire Brigade, succumbed to his injuries after a portion of a tree at Nariman Point fell on his back earlier this monsoon. His spinal cord badly damaged, he was rushed to a private hospital, but was not admitted as the hospital authorities demanded a deposit fee.
"He was severely injured, but the hospital refused to admit him without a deposit. His colleagues spent 20 minutes there, arguing with the officials. He was finally admitted after his colleagues pooled in whatever money they had at the time. The wasted time proved fatal," Sangrulkar says, going through photographs of Mohite, who lost his life on June 5. "Policemen can get admitted in private hospitals if they get injured in any incident on duty. Is a fireman's duty any less dangerous than a policeman's?" she asks.

Now, however, the BMC administration says firemen across the city will hopefully not have to cough up deposit money to get admitted to private hospitals with any work-related injury. According to Chief Fire Officer Anil Sawant, firemen will be soon issued 'smart cards' so that cases like that of Abhay Mohite do not occur again. The proposal for the 'smart card' system has been submitted by the Fire Department to the BMC administration.

However, a smart card is not the only thing that the city's bravehearts need. "We still get a risk allowance of Rs 50 per month. And there is no insurance coverage from the department in case of anything that happens to us while on duty," says one fireman, not wishing to be named.

Another fireman, also preferring to remain anonymous, says: "I suffered burn injuries during a fire-fighting operation last year and as we have no provisions for insurance or medical benefits, my seniors and colleagues contributed to raise the money needed to get me treated at a hospital specialising in burn injuries. I am still struggling with the medical bills. How much more can I rely on the generosity of my comrades?"

However, Sangrulkar has not given up the fight. "The department has offered a compensation for our loss, but that's not the end of this matter. I am being helped by the Fire and Safety Association of India (FSAI) to initiate a dialogue with the Fire Brigade to do something about the rights of the firemen. Hopefully, things will improve," she adds.

Chief Fire Officer Anil Sawant said apart from the proposal to issue smart cards, plans to increase the risk allowance have also received administrative approval. "It will soon be tabled before the standing committee after which it will be implemented within the next few months," Sawant said.

Sawant added that firemen are presently entitled to a risk allowance of Rs 50 per month, or Rs 500 for senior officers. Sawant said firemen will now be entitled to rs 500 per month too. "We want allowance for officers to be around Rs 3,000, and have proposed so," he said. The fire department's employees, however, will not get any State insurance. "They all have private life insurance. There was a proposal of group insurance for the firemen, but that proposal was rejected," Sawant added.

Heading: Missing Indians find a helping hand abroad - Indian Express
Content:
Pipped by Taare Zameen Par as India's official entry for foreign-language category, Tingya will still make the trip as emotional producer vows to go all the way with film about a boy and a bull

Critically acclaimed Marathi film Tingya, which lost out to Aamir Khan's Taare Zameen Par in the race to be India's official entry into the foreign language category at the 81st Academy Awards, will now be sent to the Oscars as an independent entry.

Tingya, directed by debutant director Mangesh Hadawale, is a film about an emotional love story between a bull and a boy, set in the backdrop of Maharashtra's agrarian crisis. The film has won several accolades at both national and international film festivals. The producer of the film, Ravi Rai, told Newsline he will pitch the film independently to the Academy. "This is a very emotional move for me. I have sailed with the film when no one was there to back it. Today, the film has reached this level so we want it to go a little further," Rai said.

He candidly added that he doesn't know the road ahead on how to go about pitching the film as an independent entrant. "There are a lot of things I'm not aware of on how to go about the independent entry submissions I'll figure it out in a week's time," he said.

For a film which was rejected by 42 producers, the remarkable journey of bagging 37 awards globally has been a phenomenal achievement, Rai said.

On the Film Federation of India jury's decision to choose Taare Zameen Par, Rai made it amply clear that he had no feeling of "being cheated". "My reaction was nothing like I was cheated or anything of that sort. Fortunately, unlike last year, this year's films were very competent, making it difficult for the jury to take a pick," he said.

Interestingly, Taare Zameen Par was Rai's own personal favourite. "Taare¿remains my favourite and I'm genuinely very happy for them as they deserve to be there. It's indeed very pleasing to see a star as big as Aamir Khan coming out to make a film on dyslexia, which even I was unaware of till I watched the movie," he said.

Earlier, Shwaas, directed by another debutant director debutant Sandeep Sawant, was India's official entry to the 2004 Oscars and was ranked 6th at the Academy Awards in the Best Foreign Language Film category. It is widely agreed that films like Shwaas and Tingyahave been instrumental in reviving Marathi cinema, attracting not only Maharashtian audiences but others too.

According to Rai, the jury debated over two hours on the final two films on the list — Taare Zameen Par and Tingya. "What I learnt from those who were witness to the discussions is that every aspect of the two films was discussed and debated in great detail by the jury members, including the child artistes," he said. Ultimately, Tingya lost on grounds of "technical finesse".

Asked about the losing factor, he said: "I don't want to get into it¿there is bound to be a difference between a Rs 27-lakh film and Rs 50-crore film."

Ironically, Tingya pipped Taare Zameen Par and Shahrukh Khan-starrer Chak De India at the MAMI International Film Festival's awards. Rai also plans to screen the film for President Pratibha Patil in the coming week.

However, Rai admitted there was no support from the Government of Maharashtra even for a film in Marathi that depicts the condition of the state.

Jittery about the way forward, he said: "Don't know what will happen, but what's important is that the honour should come to India."

Heading: HC orders demolition of encroachments on Mafatlal, govt lands - Indian Express
Content:
Cathy Shreedhar, human rights activist in US, helped trace students after Ike hit US island

Hurricane Ike that hit Cuba, United States and Haiti leaving behind a trail of death and destruction should have been merely a news item for 48-year-old Laxman Mahajik, a resident of Alibaug. But for him, it was much more than that as he was concerned about his son in the island of Galveston in Texas since Ike was heading towards the island at a breakneck speed of over 100 mph. Mahajik's 20-year-old son Rohan was in Galveston along with four other students of the Pune-based All India Shri Shivaji Memorial Hotel Management and Catering Technology since June 2008.

The last telephonic conversation Rohan had with his family was on 11 September, 2008, the day the authorities had stepped up the evacuation of people in the island. For a week after Ike started lashing the island, there was no communication from Rohan and four other students — Pradnya Gidha and Manjusha Wadkar from Thane, and Padyumna Pokish and Puneet Thakkar from Pune. They were stationed at the St Louis Resort for a four-month long training in catering management. Ironically, training in hotel management during disasters was also a part of the course.

Mahajik, who works for the RCF, tried to contact his son at the St Louis Resort in Galveston.
