Heading: Screen test - Indian Express
Content:
With five books and more than a hundred exhibitions on aerial photography, Gopal Bodhe continues with his mission to document the mesmerising vistas of the country

His eyes have glanced past more than a million awesome scenarios not only to revel in their picturesque splendour but also to capture their captivating charisma. For he is the one whose love for the heritage of his country, makes him take the lead in making the memory of these wonders last an eternity. At 61, Gopal Bodhe with clinical efficiency progresses towards achieving his mission – to document the heritage of the country. And to Bodhe who has been clicking pictures since he was eight the word is not only confined to forts and monuments, it goes beyond them encompassing the topography, geology and the sea change that it is witnessing today.

"Photography has been, and continues to be, an important method for understanding our industry, recreation, and natural landscape. As time passes, the contemporary photograph becomes a historical record and provides a window to the past. That is what I am dedicated towards, to keep this window of past always open so that people can have a glimpse of what there country used to be once upon a time and how it is now," says Bodhe who is also listed in the Limca Book of World Records for the first ever exhibition on aerial photography in India.

Bodhe's five books housing his visual collection are the testimony of the transition the country underwent, every photograph serving as a visual document bringing to the forefront the changes that till now were taken for granted. Flipping through them, one comes across pictures that surprise and shake you out of your reverie, to sit back and notice the changes around.

In his third book he documents the on–the-verge-of extinction relics, the light houses who are losing their identity in the era of GPS trackers. " Lighthouses have now become a once-upon-a-time story because of these new navigational techniques coming up. I wanted to preserve their glory as it used to be, so I clicked their pictures." Lighthouses around which the romance of many poems revolved and the suspense of many thrillers got a vivid expression find their abode in his books to rest in peace until a lover of art leafs through the pages to enliven its memories.

As one book strives to revive the spirit of the lighthouse his most recent release Mumbai – A view from Heavens stores 12 years of his work, unfolding the many layers of transition that the metropolis has gone through. "You can see in that book how the metropolis has changed in the past 12 years. How traffic used to be when the JJ flyover was not there and how it looks now when the flyover dominates the scene. Also, you can see how the green areas in many places have been compromised to make roads ."

Bodhe, who began as a solitary reaper in this field, feels a love for the art should be cultivated in youngsters. "I feel people should come forward to get into this field so that everyone comes to know how beautiful our country is and starts respecting our heritage," he signs off.

Heading: Talk the walk - Indian Express
Content:
Taare Zameen Par or Tingya... What's your choice for the Oscars?

Aamir Kahan's much accalaimed Taare Zameen Par is now India's official entry to the Oscars. But Mangesh Hadawale's Tingya, a story of the relationship between a little boy and his bull amid the issue of farmer suicides in Maharashtra, is also getting ready to woo the nominations with producer Ravi Rai having decided to take his film as an independent entry. Here's asking a cross section of people which film stands a better chance at the awards.

Milind Soman
actor
Well that's a tough question! I've seen both Tingya and Taare Zameen Par and I feel both are crafted equally well and cannot be compared on any terms be it acting, directing or story. Both films involve intense human emotions. It all depends on the jury this year and what they are looking for in international cinema. As both the films are going for the foreign language film category, I wish both would get nominated, as they are in different languages.

Suparna Gangal
short film director
I think Taare Zameen Par is the stronger contender. It had the best chance to be nominated. The story of Taare Zameen Par is intense and the content is superb. It can touch the heart of any individual irrespective of age and place. Besides, when you take a film abroad promotions play a very important role, and Aamir Khan has taken his films there earlier; this is his third time so he knows how to go about with things.

Ishani Nirgudkar
executive
I think subject wise both the films are brilliant. I have seen both the films and the two of them have a message to give to its audience. As Tingya deals with the grave reality of agrarian issues of Maharashtra, Taare Zameen Par tells a story of a boy who's parents just want him to get good grades. Taare Zameen Par deals with a much common problem. This film gives a message to the parents as well as the education system. Also, Aamir Khan who is a better-known face at the international level. This being his third time at Oscars he would know better on how to do promotions for his film. So I feel it has a better chance.

Chandrashekar Joshi
film research officer, FTII
Taare Zameen Par has a better chance at the awards not only because of its story line but also the treatment of production. Besides, the subject has been portrayed beautifully. Tingya is also a very good film but Taare Zameen Par appeals to everyone. The International audience and the Oscar jury would not only see the technical excellence and expertise but will also see how deep rooted is the subject in the respective country and would also relate it to their criteria.

Abhijeet Khandkekar
media person
If we see technically, the Indian jury selected Taare Zameen Par over Tingya due to technical finesse and I think we should trust the experts as they are judging as to what would appeal the international audience and for the benefit of Indian film industry. I have seen both the films and both are very good subject wise. Although both have been created very beautifully, I feel Taare Zameen Par has a universal appeal, as the subject is not restricted to any area or zone.

Namrata Dhotre
student
I think Tingya should win. If the entry is going from India, and if the nation has to be depicted in its true sense then I think the essence of its life, people and culture must find representation in the film. Taking this into consideration Tingya definitely has an upper hand.

Ankush Chowdhary
actor
It is difficult to comment as both the films are extremely well made. As both deal with different subjects they can't be judged from a particular point. I think both have an equal chance as they have left a very good impact on the audience.

Heading: 76 yrs after Poona Pact, BJP woos minorities - Indian Express
Content:
The runway sets the pulse racing for the older of the tantalising model twins

It isn't often that we read Tupur Chatterjee's name separated from her sister Tapur. But during the just concluded India Couture Week, Tupur tells us that it was a conscious decision on their part to not do the same shows. "Once in a way, it is nice to see us separately. Only then probably people see the difference between us," she says, as the make-up artiste does a good job of making her eyes look dramatic for Pallavi Jaikishan's show. But do people confuse between the two? "All the time. But now we are used to it. If you spend a couple of days with us, you will know the difference in our facial structure and also our personalities," she says, as she enters the green room.

The backstage seems to be the centre of all activity right now with make-up artistes and hairstylists getting their act right, caterers serving some diet food, event organisers running helter-skelter to get the stage ready, choreographers doling out instructions, models dabbing on some rouge and gloss and an in-house photographer capturing these moments. Tupur, who is older by 12 minutes, feels the backstage is a quintessential part of their life because it is here that they spend most of their time dressing up, making friends, practicing their walk and, sometimes, thinking of innovative ways of killing time. Other models, who are doing similar stuff, hover around graciously as Tupur fields simple questions. "In our profession, the waiting period is the biggest drawback. Models make it to the venue at least seven hours in advance. If we could cut down on the waiting period, we would look so much fresher," she says sipping on water.

In spite of being in the profession for eight years, her enthusiasm is still in place. Even today she looks excited about wearing yet another designer ensemble and sauntering down the ramp. "I get very excited but I am never nervous of walking the ramp. If the ramp is slippery or has paper bits, it does get a little scary," says the 28-year-old, while practicing her sequence of steps. And with the couture week being more elaborate in terms of settings, choreography and clothes, the anxiety becomes two-fold.

The sisters have had a firm finger on the fashion pulse of the city. But Tupur, a graduate in Biology, feels that the industry has grown massively over the last couple of years. "Today there are more international designs in the market. There is a Western feel to Indian wear," she says as she points to the outfit she wears. "Also the fashion shows are more organised now, unlike earlier when you did not know what was happening."

But for this granddaughter of Hrishikesh Mukherjee, one of the most revered filmmakers of the industry, Bollywood is still a distant calling. "It is those two minutes on the ramp that make me feel like a queen. Also, most of your dreams of wearing the best clothes available in the country get fulfilled." No wonder then, that between shouts of 'Hurry Up' and 'Find the damn hair pin' in the green room, Tupur manages to hold on to her nerve.

Heading: City hospitals find two ways to keep clean - Indian Express
Content:
ON DEAF EARS: Ambedkar's grandson not interested in proposal; Congress not even invited to meet to commemorate historic event

BJP national secretary Gopinath Munde on Wednesday urged the leaders of minority communities to join hands with his party, while speaking at the convention to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the Poona Pact.

Bharipa Bahujan Mahasangh (BBM) leader Prakash Ambedkar, however, did not reciprocate to the call, though he justified the demand for reservation for Maratha community. As for the Congress and the NCP, they were not even invited to the celebration that was attended by over 5,000 followers of the RPI-Ambedkar faction.

Prakash Ambedkar is the grandson of Babasahed Ambedkar, who had signed the Poona Pact with Mahatma Gandhi at the Yerawada Jail in 1932, setting the ball rolling on what later came to be reservations for the backward classes in independent India.

"We should not think of the past and instead work together to ensure social justice to all," Munde said addressing the convention organised by BBM at the B J Medical Ground.

There is a need to continue the fight started by Babasaheb Ambedkar against discrimination of the backward classes, Munde said, adding: "The BBM leader should take forward the movement of social justice launched by Ambedkar and we will always be there to back him."

The discrimination of backward class is still prevalent in the society and needs to be checked, Munde said while welcoming the Bhandara session court judgment earlier in the day awarding the death sentence to six accused and life imprisonment to two accused in Khairlanji case.

The BJP leader said the voice against discrimination being raised now is only due to the movement launched by Babasaheb Ambedkar in the past. "I am regular, unlike other political leaders, in paying homage to Babasaheb Ambedkar on his death anniversary on December 6," Munde said.

Prakash Ambedkar said the future political battle should not be based on emotions but on intellectual grounds. The strategy of ruling parties, especially the Congress, has been to play politics of hatred, he said. Many political leaders use double standards towards the backward class by merely showing sympathy for the depressed class but not doing anything for their uplift, he said.

The Poona Pact made history by providing reservations for the backward class, Ambedkar said, adding the fight for justice has not yet finished.

Atrocities in the name of caste should stop, he said, adding that the Khairlanji case judgment would be a message to those victimising the backward class. "There should be many more such punishments for those perpetrating atrocities against the backward class community members," Ambedkar said.

"Babasaheb had mentioned the Maratha community in the list of communities for which reservations should be made, but there was opposition from a few leaders of the same community. It is now they have realised that they are also in the minority," he said.

Many leaders, one thought
* Annasaheb Patil: We need to strengthen a front for the backward classes. Munde should quit the BJP and lead that front.
* Ganpatrao Deshmukh, Peasants and Workers Party: Backward classes needed to work together.
* Raja Dhale, BBM: But for the Poona Pact, atrocities against backward classes would have been rampant.
* Mustaffa FarukiL, Jamaat-e-Islami: We need unity among the many organisations fighting for the cause of minorities.

Heading: Sassoon plans to get sweeping  outsourced - Indian Express
Content:
Medical waste packed offto Satara

Pune, for long struggling with its garbage, has found a solution to get rid of its hospital waste, at least. For the last couple of days, the city's medical waste has been sent by road to Satara, at least two hours away.

Satara district collector Vikas Deshmukh said he was unaware of the development. "The association of doctors has started a facility three months ago for disposing of waste but that is generated in Satara," he said.

As many as 530 hospitals, nine blood banks, 115 pathological laboratories and 250 dispensaries and clinics generate around 1,200 kg of biomedical waste every day. This was being collected from 250 points in the city by Sun Enviro Limited that was operating the incinerator at the Kailash crematorium. With the biomedical waste disposal facility at the crematorium shut down following a blast two weeks ago, doctors had struggled to dispose of syringes, needles, blood soaked cotton swabs, bandages and even body parts, all which were piling up at city hospitals.

Municipal commissioner Praveensinh Pardeshi said Satara was only an interim arrangement. The Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPB), he said, has permitted the Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) to dispose of the waste at three places - Pimpri Chinchwad, Talegaon and now Satara.

The PMC had put the ball in the court of the MPCB as the latter had not allowed the civic body to use the incinerator on the Kailash crematorium campus.

"Following the blast a fortnight ago, we decided to shut down the facility and allowed the PMC to utilise alternative facilities as a stop gap arrangement for two months," said P K Mirashe, regional officer for the MPCB in Pune.

Dr P S Dhaigude, chief medical officer of the PMC, said they were working out alternative arrangements but in the meantime the MPCB had allowed them to send the city's medical waste to Satara.

The PMC had also urged PCMC to dispose of its waste and temporarily hired the services of Passco Environment Solutions Limited for this. Pradeep Mulay, director of Passco, said they were able to collect only about 400 kg of biomedical waste from Pune.

"The medical waste generated in PCMC is nearly 550 kg a day and the incinerator set up at YCM Hospital at Chinchwad can take an extra load of 300 kg. The Talegaon waste disposal facility accommodates another 150 kg," Mulay said.

Heading: Batons or no batons, traffic cops remain vulnerable to attack - Indian Express
Content:
With shortage of staff plaguing the 1,300-bed Sassoon General Hospital, the task of maintaining cleanliness is about to be outsourced, The decision was taken following a high level meeting held in Pune and chaired by Dilip Walse Patil, Medical Education Minister, to take stock of the problems at the State government-run hospital, including lack of security on its campus and shortage of staff.

Kamal Dhole Patil, an MLA attending the meeting, had raised the issue of staff shortage and the necessity to fill up vacant posts. According to Walse Patil, there are at least 104 Class IV and other posts lying vacant.

Officials at Sassoon hospital said there was a dearth of people to perform basic duties like sweeping or cleaning the wards. They demanded that such cleaning functions should be outsourced from elsewhere as the hospital was shortstaffed and unable to do it.

Walse Patil told The Indian Express that orders have also been issued to pull down illegal hoardings at the B J Medical College ground near Nehru Memorial Hall, following objections raised by officials and MLAs present at the meeting.Dr Nirmala Borade, Dean, Sassoon General hospital, said that the ground, used by students of B J Medical College for sporting activities, is also let out for commercial purposes like holding exhibitions and other functions.

Of late, several hoardings have been set up for display without the permission of Sassoon officials. Walse Patil directed the officials to use police force to pull down the hoardings that are not sanctioned and even evict people who were residing unlawfully at the ground.

The meeting also scrutinised whether funds granted by the state for introducing new equipment at the hospital have been utilised. Health secretary Bhushan Gagrani, Director of Medical Education and Research W B Tayade along with MLAs Vallabh Benke, Chandrakant Chhajed, Balasaheb Shivarkar and others were present.

Heading: Puran polis, made in Mauritius with tips from Pune - Indian Express
Content:
Constable, warden whipped with belts

A gang of eight, most of them history-sheeters and under the influence of alcohol, whipped a traffic constable and a traffic warden with belts at Lulla Nagar junction on Monday evening. Despite having been provided batons, traffic policemen continue to be the victims of attacks; the police are now thinking of stricter measures.

The traffic control branch maintains a record of the number of attacks on police personnel on duty. Between January and September, the police arrested 48 persons for 13 such attacks.

The attack on constable Navnath Kale of Kondhwa traffic control division and traffic warden Rahul Gire at Lulla Junction is now being considered a major one. Police said a group of youth misbehaved with the warden around 7.15 pm, leading to heated arguments and then the assaualt. When the constable tried to pacify the youths, he too was thrashed.

Kale lodged a complaint with the Kondhwa police, who arrested seven of the eight.

"Some of them were earlier arrested for murder and rioting. The court later acquitted them. They were drunk when they attacked the traffic warden and constable," said senior police inspector R B Gaikar. Deputy Commissioner of Police (traffic) Manoj Patil said that incident is being treated as serious.

"We are planning strict action against attackers. At a meeting of top-ranked police officers, we decided that all attack on traffic cops would be investigated by senior inspectors. Besides, I and zonal deputy commissioners will personally ensure that attackers are arrested and booked under stringent sections," Patil said.

Some traffic wardens, whose job is monitor traffic flow, allegedly act as law-enforcers and ask for licences and pollution certificates from commuters, which has upset many. A few wardens were also seen carrying batons given to the traffic policemen. When The Indian Express clicked the photograph of one such warden, he returned the baton to the traffic cop.

Heading: Five faces of terror - Indian Express
Content:
21 women from city SHGs to travel abroad and train teachers how to prepare various Indian delicacies

Do not be surprised if you suddenly encounter a Mauritian teacher preparing puran polis or motichoor laddoos. Twenty-one women from different self help groups (SHGs) of Pune are visiting Mauritius to teach school and college teachers of that country how to prepare various Indian delicacies.

"We have shortlisted about 35 types of products, including items like besan laddoos, artificial jewellery, wedding bags, jewellery bags, salwar-kameez and sari blouses," said Deepti Chaudhari, former mayor and president of the Manasi Mahila Unnati Kendra (women's development centre) which is coordinating the visit. "A group of 30 to 35 Mauritian teachers will be trained in each product," she added.

Rupali Jadhav of Jagruti SHG, Dhankawdi, which specialises in preparing murals, just can't wait for the tour to start. "I will be carrying moulds of Ganapati idols of various sizes to teach the Mauritian teachers idol-making," she informed excitedly. There was a similar sense of eager anticipation in Rupali Jadhav of Tanishka SHG, who will teach jewellery-bag making, and Vasudha Kale of Siddhivinayak SHG, Talegaon Dabhade, who will teach preparation of food items.

Asked whether the language barrier would prove a problem for the Pune women during their Mauritius trip, Chaudhari replied that they would be taking a couple of English to Marathi translators with them but there would not be much of a problem.

"One of the reasons we agreed to go was because we found a large Indian population there. Also, the Mauritius Marathi Federation has extended its help to us," Chaudhari said.

In May a group from Manasi had organised an exhibition of such products in Mauritius, which had received an overwhelming response. Now the Mauritius government has extended a second invitation — not just for the exhibition and sale of the products but also for training of Mauritian women in preparing them, Chaudhari added.

This will be the first foreign trip for these women, who have never ventured even out of their city or state.

"I feel that the women should learn about the attractive and sustainable packaging methods needed for the international market, as well as marketing skills," Chaudhari said. Of the 21 women, 16 have got their passports and tickets. They will leave on Monday and return on October 5.

Heading: BMC to rope in doctors against sex selection - Indian Express
Content:
'Timer expert' among catches

Mohammed Arif Shaikh (28), one of the five arrested by the Mumbai Police, is reported to be an "expert" in setting up electric circuits, responsible for setting up the timers in the bombs that caused the recent blasts across the country.

The police suspect he could be the person who assembled and set the digital timers in Surat too. While Arif, who was reportedly trained in a "hostile country", is reported to be an expert at electric circuits, he is said to be honing his skills in "digital timers".

Among the recent blasts for which the Indian Mujahideen has claimed credit, it was only in Surat bombs and Bangalore where digital timers, in the form of Thailand-manufactured Motorola microchips, were used. All the nine bombs in Bangalore exploded.

The Mumbai crime branch believe that the five alleged Indian Mujahideen operatives, all natives of Azamgarh, were involved in assisting in assembling and executing major terror blasts across the country since 2005. Officials said Arif's interrogation could help them understand the kind of timers that were used in the train serial blasts in Mumbai on July 11, 2006, which claimed 187 lives.

Experts believe that the July 11 blasts were actually triggered by digital timers, and not through quartz timers as recorded in the chargesheet. "There were very crucial microchips recovered from the blast spots. The Mumbai Police recorded it as quartz timers though no pieces of watch were ever recovered. Arif should throw light now, if he was indeed a part of that group," said a bomb expert who inspected the blast sites on July 11.

"The concept of digital timers exists among Jammu and Kashmir militants," said an expert with the NSG.

Joint Commissioner of Police (Crime Branch) Rakesh Maria said that the group was also behind the Varanasi blasts in 2006, Shramjeevi Express blast in 2005 as well as the Hyderabad blasts. Quartz timers were used in all these cases.

...THE OTHER FOUR
* Mohammed Sadiq Israr Sheikh, 32
Identified as the co-founder of the Indian Mujahideen, he is from Sanjarpur in Azamgarh. Sadiq is reported to be the man who "controlled" New Delhi's serial blasts, through key executor Atif who was killed in the Jamia Nagar encounter. Sadiq had settled in Mumbai's Cheetah Camp area, a predominantly Muslim slum colony. "He worked in Mumbai as a programme engineer in an electronic company," said Joint Commissioner of Police Rakesh Maria, describing him as the "brains behind footsoldiers like Atif". Sadiq received "training in terror activities from a hostile country" on two occasions. He was wanted by the Delhi Police too.
* Mohammed Ansar Sheikh, 31
A native of Sanjarpur in Azamgarh, Ansar is a software engineer. He was living in Cheetah Camp near Trombay for several months now. Initial investigations point to his involvement in the Indian Mujahideen as the man who provided software knowledge to the terror module. He was arrested from Chembur.
* Afzal Mutalib Usmani, 32
Also hailed from Azamgarh. Was reportedly responsible for the theft of four cars from Navi Mumbai, which were used in the Ahmedabad and Surat attacks. Arrested from Mhow in UP, Afzal is also reported to have placed the explosive-laden vehicles at Ahmedabad's Civil Hospital and Bazar Peth. He has a crime record — the first case against him was an attempt to murder in 1996, at Shivaji Nagar police station, Mumbai. He is also wanted in a MCOCA case where he is charged with being an associate of the Fazl-ul-Rehman gang. Of the five arrested, he is the only one to have a crime record.
* Mohammed Zakir Sheikh, 28
Originally from Azamgarh, Zakir, a scrap deal, had settled down in Bhiwandi. He is reported to have received training outside the country in 2004, before he returned to Azamgarh. He later moved to Bhiwandi, on the outskirts of Mumbai, in Thane district, where he set up a scrap dealing business that took him to Surat often. He is alleged to have been in the team which conducted a recce in Gujarat, and helped the module in planting bombs at various locations. He was picked up from Bhiwandi on Tuesday night.

Also wanted
* Roshan Khan
Hailing from Karnataka, Roshan Khan is believed to be "one of the founding members" of the Indian Mujhaideen. Roshan Khan is high up in the Indian Mujaideen hierarchy along with Sadiq.
* Ameer Razaq
Additional Commissioner of Police (Crime Branch) Deven Bharti said Sadiq was in constant touch with a man in Pakistan named Ameer Razaq, who appears to be controlling the group. "We have sufficient proof including telephone details to prove that he is handling the operation from Pakistan.

Heading: Will 400-yr-old Haji Ali dargah become Mumbai’s own Taj? - Indian Express
Content:
The BMC, in response to the falling sex ratio at birth since the last population census, has set up a body — Doctors Against Sex Selection — where doctors, radiologists, sonologists will register themselves and participate in the campaign against sex detection. "We are now setting up a Doctors Against Sex Selection forum, which will consist of doctors and radiologists who will volunteer to give information," informed Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal (Prevention) Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Officer In-Charge Asha Advani.

Speaking at workshop organised by NGO Laadli on the occasion of SAARC Girl Child Day, she said, "Doctors can secretly inform us if they hear of any sex selection occurring and we will take action. We are roping in the police and NGOs, too, for the project."

Last month a team had conducted surprise checks on clinics and sealed almost a dozen machines.

From 923 girls born in the city for every 1,000 boys at the time of the 2001 census, the BMC registered the birth of 921 girls for every 1,000 boys last year. While the eastern suburbs recorded 912 female births for every 1,000 boys, the island city and western suburbs fared marginally better with 925 girls per 1,000 boys born in the same period. Pockets like Parel recorded the birth of 1,275 girls for each 1,000 boys in 2005 but the ratio dropped in 2007 to 885 girls per 1,000 boys. The rates in the Tony towns of Malabar Hill, Walkeshwar and Chowpatty have fallen drastically from 967 girls born per 1,000 boys in 2005 to 895 girls in 2007.

This year the BMC has registered 1,386 sonography clinics and renewed registration to 587 clinics. Ninety clinics have been sealed so far for failing to following the PCPNDT Act.

"We have ensured that machines and doctors are registered. We have also told companies that they should not sell sonography machines to unregistered centres," Advani added.

Heading: HC admits Mulund blast accused plea on illegal detention - Indian Express
Content:
Conversion of cement concrete structure into marble wonder begins with demolition of one minaret

The 400-year-old Haji Ali dargah, nestled like a pearl in the greyish Arabian sea, began a makeover journey today which will metamorphose the cement concrete structure into a sparkling white marble wonder. Two years later, when the reconstruction work is complete, the holy shrine will give the feel of a Taj right in Mumbai's brakish sea water.

The dargah will be beautified with first and second quality white marble, which will be brought from Makrana, Rajasthan, the same place from which marble for the Taj Mahal had been brought. "The original structure, which was made of cement concrete, will now be of white marble. It will be a little Taj Mahal-like structure in the sea," said architect Chetan Raikar.

The marble frames will be made in Rajasthan and will only be fixed at the mosque, to save time and avoid construction complexities. While the first phase reconstruction will include the mosque, phase 2 will involve the sanitarium building.

The structural upgradation of one of the most prominent shrines in the country began with the bringing down of one of the minarets. The stone-laying ceremony for the reconstruction will be conducted in the second week of October.

The reconstruction has been in the pipeline for four years but was awaiting the necessary approvals, including CRZ and heritage department clearances. The final order was received a fortnight ago and the demolition began today. "Part of a Minara and a chatri (umbrella) have been taken up for demolition," Raikar added. Spread around 3,000 sq feet in the middle of the Arabian sea, the mosque stands 14 feet tall. During the reconstruction, it will be raised a bit higher to 18 feet by Structwell Designers and Consultants Pvt Ltd, which is in charge of the Rs 9.2 crore project.

The reconstruction and demolition work will be carried out simultaneously. During this period, the movement of devotees and visitors will be controlled — they will be allowed to go inside the mosque but entry will be restricted near the work area.

"Once complete, the structure will be better than even the Taj." Around 35,000 cubic feet of marble will be used for the reconstruction," Raikar informed.

The shrine of Pir Haji Ali Shah Baba dates back to the 14th century and the present structure was constructed a little over 100 years ago. However, constant erosion and salty winds have dilapidated the building, which is visited by around 80,000 people every week.

Content:
In a major relief for Mulund blast accused, Adnan Mulla, the Bombay High Court on Wednesday admitted his petition regarding his illegal detention in 2002-03. The court has admitted the petition with regard to the issue of illegal detention and prosecution of police officials.

The court has now directed Mulla to make the three police officers, ACP Ramakant Padwal, police inspectors RV Vanmane and Nitin Patil, respondants to the petition.

The officers were indicted in a judicial inquiry carried out by the Principal Judge of the Sessions Court. Mulla also sought his exoneration from the blast case in view of the illegal detention on the grounds that there was evidence to show that he was subsequently made an accused in the case.

The court, however, asked him to approach trial court with the plea. The court had earlier asked the state government to go through the report regarding the alleged illegal detention of Mulla and inform the court on the action taken by the state on it. The court was hearing a petition filed by blast accused Adnan Mulla, which alleged that he was illegally detained for 35 days by police. The court had earlier ordered a probe by a judicial officer into the illegal detention.

According to Mulla's lawyer Mubin Solkar, the court will now hear it finally and decide on the prosecution of the officers. The court had earlier held that there was some substance in the report and had directed public prosecutor Satish Borulkar or the Advocate General to appear in the case.                                                                            Mulla and 19 other accused have been charged with triggering chain of explosions at Ghatkopar, Mulund, Bombay Central and Vile Parle in 2002-03.
